analysis.one_liner: Directs the FTC to write rules against telemarketing fraud and lets states and consumers sue violators.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill by voice vote in October 1990, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Federal Trade Commission to write rules for phone-based sales: refunds when goods don't arrive on time, the right to cancel an order, limits on when unsolicited calls can be made, a ban on computer-generated robocalls that won't let you hang up, and recordkeeping requirements. It also would have let state attorneys general sue fraudulent telemarketers on behalf of residents, let the FTC pursue wrongdoers more aggressively, and given the FTC a public clearinghouse where consumers could check on telemarketing firms. The Senate passed it unanimously by voice vote, but the House never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers targeted by phone sales scams — disproportionately older Americans — gain refund rights, cancellation rights, calling-hour limits, and a government office to check complaints. State attorneys general gain a new federal tool to sue fraudulent telemarketers on behalf of their residents, and the FTC gains subpoena and contempt powers to pursue repeat offenders.

how_it_helps.text: Orders the FTC to write rules requiring refunds when goods or services bought by phone are not delivered on time, and giving buyers a period to cancel an order.

Requires the FTC to consider limits on the hours when unsolicited sales calls can be made, a ban on computer-generated calls that the recipient cannot terminate, and recordkeeping requirements for telemarketers.
Lets any state's attorney general sue in federal court on behalf of residents to stop a pattern of telemarketing that violates FTC rules, to enforce compliance, and to win damages for residents.

Expands FTC investigative power: courts can summon parties located anywhere, civil investigative demands now cover physical evidence like products and recordings, and financial records can be disclosed without notice to a fraud suspect if assets are likely to be moved or destroyed.
Requires the FTC to set up a public clearinghouse that answers inquiries about telemarketing firms and routes complaints to the right federal or state agency.
Extends the FTC's false-advertising ban to services, not just food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics, and gives the FTC authority to bring criminal contempt actions against violators of court orders.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing businesses that would face new federal rules, refunds, recordkeeping, and lawsuits from state attorneys general; the bill leaves out catalog mailers and securities and futures firms, so the cost falls on the phone-sales industry it does cover.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action is narrow: a suit is only allowed if the amount in controversy exceeds $50,000 in actual damages for each affected person, so an individual consumer cheated of a few thousand dollars gets no private lawsuit under this Act.
The core provisions — the FTC rulemaking, state AG suits, and private suits — expire five years after enactment, forcing Congress to reauthorize them to keep any protection in place.

The bill carves out whole industries: catalog sales are excluded from the definition of telemarketing if the seller meets several conditions, and securities and futures transactions by firms regulated by the SEC or CFTC are entirely exempt — areas where 'boiler-room' phone fraud was already a known problem.
The life care home industry, a subject of consumer complaints, receives only a study and a report to Congress within 24 months, with no rules and no deadline for the FTC to decide on rulemaking.

The bill preempts nothing but also blocks private and state suits against a defendant once the FTC has filed its own action over the same alleged violations, concentrating enforcement in the agency's hands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real — refund rights, cancellation rights, calling-hour limits, and a state-level enforcement tool against fraud that mainly harms older and lower-income households. But the design is weaker than it looks: the $50,000-per-person threshold makes private suits nearly unreachable for the individual victims fraud most often creates, the catalog and securities exemptions leave open large fraud channels, and the five-year sunset makes the whole framework temporary. A fair reading is that this is a useful, industry-acceptable first step rather than a tough crackdown.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously by voice vote on October 23, 1990, but the House never brought it up, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced April 23, 1990 by Senator Bryan of Nevada, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held subcommittee hearings on May 2, 1990.
The Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment on July 26, 1990, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate passed the bill with amendments by voice vote on October 23, 1990 and sent it to the House.
The House took no action on the bill for the rest of the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991, so the bill never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketers, including fraudulent operators, were better off: no federal telemarketing rules, state-AG enforcement framework, or FTC clearinghouse took effect from this bill. Consumers defrauded by phone scams gained nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor advanced it through a Democratic-run Senate, which passed it unanimously by voice vote; the record shows no opposition from any member, only House inaction.

industries.note: The bill subjects phone-sales operations to FTC refund, cancellation, calling-hour, and recordkeeping rules, with state attorneys general empowered to sue fraudulent operators on behalf of consumers. Legitimate firms bear compliance costs; fraudulent ones face the real loss.

The bill exempts securities and futures transactions by SEC- and CFTC-regulated firms entirely, keeping 'boiler-room' investment fraud pitches outside the FTC telemarketing rules that would otherwise reach them.

Sellers who mail catalogs meeting specific conditions are excluded from the definition of telemarketing, so they avoid the refund, cancellation, and recordkeeping rules even when consumers place follow-up calls to order.

Banks that lose money to telemarketing fraud are given standing to sue under the Act, but they also face the requirement to disclose customer financial records to courts without notice when fraud assets are likely to be dissipated.
The industry escapes any rulemaking in the bill; it receives only an FTC study and a report to Congress within 24 months, leaving existing practices untouched in the meantime.
